Now ready.<|end_think|>Let  

\[
F_{p}=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z ,\qquad 
\mathcal P=\{f(x)=a_{3}x^{3}+a_{2}x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0}\;|\;a_{i}\in F_{p}\}.
\]

There are  

\[
|\mathcal P| =p^{4}
\]

polynomials of degree \(\le 3\) (the zero polynomial is included; it clearly has a root).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Polynomials that vanish at a given point

For each \(c\in F_{p}\) let  

\[
A_{c}=\{f\in\mathcal P\;|\;f(c)=0\}.
\]

The condition \(f(c)=0\) is a single linear equation in the four coefficients,
hence  

\[
|A_{c}|=p^{3}.
\]

If \(c_{1}\neq c_{2}\) the two equations \(f(c_{1})=0,\;f(c_{2})=0\) are
independent, so  

\[
|A_{c_{1}}\cap A_{c_{2}}|=p^{2}.
\]

Similarly, for three distinct points  

\[
|A_{c_{1}}\cap A_{c_{2}}\cap A_{c_{3}}|=p,
\]

and for four distinct points the only polynomial that vanishes at all of them
is the zero polynomial, so  

\[
|A_{c_{1}}\cap A_{c_{2}}\cap A_{c_{3}}\cap A_{c_{4}}|=1 .
\]

If we ask for a polynomial to vanish at five or more distinct points,
the only possibility is still the zero polynomial, so the intersection size
remains \(1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Inclusion–exclusion

The set of polynomials having **at least one** root is \(\bigcup_{c\in F_{p}}A_{c}\).
Using inclusion–exclusion and the sizes just computed,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|\bigcup_{c}A_{c}\bigr|
&=\sum_{i=1}^{p}(-1)^{\,i+1}\!\!\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq F_{p}\\|C|=i}}|A_{C}|\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{4}(-1)^{i+1}\binom{p}{i}p^{\,4-i}
      \;+\;\sum_{i=5}^{p}(-1)^{i+1}\binom{p}{i}\cdot 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Recall the binomial identity \(\sum_{i=0}^{p}(-1)^{i}\binom{p}{i}=0\).
Hence  

\[
\sum_{i=5}^{p}(-1)^{i+1}\binom{p}{i}
=-\sum_{i=0}^{4}(-1)^{i}\binom{p}{i}.
\]

Putting everything together, the number of **root‑free** polynomials is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N &= p^{4}
   -\binom{p}{1}p^{3}
   +\binom{p}{2}p^{2}
   -\binom{p}{3}p
   +\binom{p}{4}  \\
  &\qquad
   -\Bigl[\binom{p}{0}
          -\binom{p}{1}
          +\binom{p}{2}
          -\binom{p}{3}
          +\binom{p}{4}\Bigr] .
\end{aligned}
\]

Simplifying (using \(\binom{p}{k}=p(p-1)\cdots(p-k+1)/k!\)) gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N&=\binom{p}{2}(p^{2}-1)-\binom{p}{3}(p-1)+(p-1)\\[2mm]
 &=\frac{p(p-1)(p^{2}-1)}{2}
   -\frac{p(p-1)^{2}(p-2)}{6}
   +(p-1)\\[2mm]
 &=\frac{2p^{4}+p^{3}-8p^{2}+11p-6}{6}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The numerator factors as \((p-1)(2p^{3}+3p^{2}-5p+6)\), so an equivalent compact
form is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
N=\frac{(p-1)\bigl(2p^{3}+3p^{2}-5p+6\bigr)}{6}}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Check

For the first few primes:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p & N \\
\hline
2 & 4\\
3 & 24\\
5 & 204\\
7 & 804\\
11& 4960
\end{array}
\]

which agrees with a direct enumeration.  

Thus the number of inequivalent integer polynomials modulo a prime \(p\) of
degree at most \(3\) that have **no** integer root modulo \(p\) is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\frac{(p-1)(2p^{3}+3p^{2}-5p+6)}{6}}
\] (equivalently \(\displaystyle \frac{2p^{4}+p^{3}-8p^{2}+11p-6}{6}\)).<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
